pages.title: About Lift Tables
pages.excerpt: What this directory covers, where its specifications come from, and how it makes money.
pages.content:
Lift Tables is an independent directory of industrial lift tables, tilters and pallet positioners sold in North America. It exists to answer one question quickly: which models can do the job, and who sells them.

What's in the directory

The directory covers 20 manufacturers, their product lines, and the model numbers, capacities, platform sizes and travel published for each one, alongside the manufacturer's own brochures and owner's manuals.

Scope is deliberate: lift tables, tilt tables, pallet positioners and elevating carts. Dock lifts, vertical reciprocating conveyors, stackers and personnel platforms are left out, even where the same manufacturers make them.

Where the specifications come from

Every product line records the manufacturer pages, catalogs and data sheets its facts came from. Specifications are copied as the manufacturer publishes them and are not adjusted, estimated or filled in. Where a manufacturer publishes no model table, the line says so rather than guessing.

Manufacturers change their models and their literature without notice. Confirm capacity, dimensions and options with the manufacturer or distributor before you buy. If you find something out of date or wrong, tell us and we will fix it.

Not affiliated with the manufacturers

Lift Tables is not affiliated with, endorsed by or authorized by any manufacturer listed here. Every brand name, model number, trademark and logo belongs to its owner and is used only to identify the equipment being described.

Product photographs and PDF documents are the manufacturers' own material. Each is credited on the page it appears on and links back to the page the manufacturer publishes it on. If you represent a manufacturer and want your photos, documents or listing changed or removed, email tim@lifttables.us and we will act on it promptly.

How the directory makes money

Distributors pay to be listed and to receive quote requests for the brands and regions they cover. Buyers pay nothing, and a manufacturer cannot pay to change how its equipment is described or ranked in the catalog. Paid distributor listings are marked as such, and their outbound links are tagged sponsored.

Contact

Questions, corrections and listing enquiries: tim@lifttables.us. See the contact page for which address to use.

pages.title: Contact
pages.excerpt: How to reach Lift Tables about quotes, listings, corrections and removal requests.
pages.content:
Lift Tables is run by Tim Statler. Email is the fastest way to reach us, and messages are usually answered within one business day.

Buying equipment

For quotes, use the quote form, or the form on any product line page so we know which model you're asking about. It reaches distributors who carry that brand. You can also email support@lifttables.us.

Listing your company

Distributors and dealers: list your company to receive quote requests for the brands and regions you cover. Questions about listings go to tim@lifttables.us.

Manufacturers

To correct a specification, update a photo or document, add a product line, or have your material removed, email tim@lifttables.us. Removal requests are acted on promptly, and nothing has to be justified to us first. We are also glad to link to the literature you would rather buyers saw.

Corrections

If a capacity, dimension or model number here doesn't match the manufacturer's current data, tell us which page and what it should say. Corrections are checked against the manufacturer's own published source.

Privacy requests

To see or delete the personal information you have sent through a form, email tim@lifttables.us. See the privacy policy for what is collected and who it goes to.

Written correspondence

Lift Tables is run remotely and takes correspondence by email. If you need to send something in writing, email tim@lifttables.us and we will give you an address for it.

pages.title: Privacy Policy
pages.excerpt: What Lift Tables collects when you request a quote or list your company, who receives it, and how to have it deleted.
pages.content:
Last updated 21 September 2026.

This policy explains what Lift Tables (lifttables.us) collects, why, and what you can do about it. It covers this website only.

Who we are

Lift Tables is an independent equipment directory run by Tim Statler. Contact: tim@lifttables.us. We are based in Indiana, United States, and handle correspondence by email; write to that address if you need somewhere to send a formal notice.

What we collect

When you request a quote we collect your name and email address, and, if you give them, your phone number, company, ZIP or postal code, the equipment category you're interested in, your timeline, and whatever you write in the message. We also record which page you sent the request from, so the distributor knows which model you mean.

When you ask to list your company we collect your company name, website, your name, email address, phone number, the brands and regions you cover, the listing you're interested in, and your message.

Automatically, our web host keeps standard server logs, and your IP address is used briefly to limit repeat form submissions. Your IP address is not stored with your request.

We do not collect payment card details on this site, and we do not ask for any sensitive personal information.

Why we use it, and who receives it

A quote request exists to be answered by someone who sells the equipment. When you send one, we pass your name, contact details and message to distributors who carry that brand — up to three of them — so they can quote you. They contact you directly, and their own privacy practices then apply to what you send them. Until distributors are listed for a brand, requests come to us and we forward them to a supplier on your behalf.

We also use what you send to reply to you, to keep a record of the request, and to understand which equipment buyers ask about. We do not sell your personal information, and we do not share it with anyone other than the distributors handling your request and the service providers below.

Service providers

The site runs on managed WordPress hosting, and email is sent through Google Workspace. These providers process data on our behalf in order to run the site and deliver messages. Visit measurement is described below.

Cookies and analytics

Since 21 September 2026 this site uses Google Analytics to count visits and see which equipment pages people read. It sets a first-party cookie in your browser so a returning visit is not counted twice, and it sends your IP address to Google, which derives an approximate location from it and does not store it. We see totals and trends; we cannot see who you are.

Google Signals and ad personalisation are both switched off in our settings, so what we measure does not feed Google’s advertising profile of you and we cannot build advertising audiences from it. The site sets no advertising cookies and loads no other third-party script — our typefaces are served from our own server rather than from Google Fonts, so simply reading a page does not hand your address to anyone else.

To stay out of it, use an ad or tracker blocker, or install Google’s opt-out browser add-on. Nothing on this site is withheld from you for doing so.

WordPress sets cookies only if you log in or leave a comment. Forms use a short-lived security token to prevent abuse.

How long we keep it

Quote and listing requests are kept for three years so we can answer follow-up questions and resolve disputes, then deleted. Ask us sooner and we will delete yours.

Your choices

Email tim@lifttables.us to get a copy of what we hold about you, correct it, or have it deleted. We will respond within 30 days. Depending on where you live, you may have rights under laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act or the GDPR, including access, deletion, correction and the right not to be discriminated against for exercising them. We honour these requests for everyone, wherever you are.

Distributors who have already received your request hold their own copy. We will tell you who they were so you can contact them.

Security

The site is served over HTTPS and requests are stored in the site's database, which only the site's administrator can read. No website can promise perfect security, but we keep access limited and software updated.

Children

This is a site for buying industrial equipment. It is not directed to children, and we do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 16.

Changes

If this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it. Material changes will be noted on this page. The most recent was on 21 September 2026, when we added Google Analytics; before that the site carried no analytics at all.

pages.title: Buying guides
pages.excerpt: Plain explanations of how lift tables are specified, written from the published specifications of 4,707 models.
pages.content: These are written for someone who has to buy a lift table and has not bought one before. Every figure in them is read from the manufacturers' own published specifications for the 4,707 models in this directory, so where a guide says most tables do something, it means most of the tables you can actually buy.

pages.title: What is a lift table?
pages.excerpt: What a lift table does, the mechanisms they are built on, how they are powered, and the four numbers that decide which one fits.
pages.content:
A lift table raises a load to a chosen height and holds it there. That is the whole of it. What makes them worth specifying carefully is that almost every industrial task involving a heavy object gets easier, faster or safer when the object is at the right height, and almost every one of them is currently done at the wrong height.

There are two separate reasons to buy one. The first is the operator: a worker who bends into a pallet or reaches over the side of a container two hundred times a shift is accumulating an injury. Raising and angling the work removes the bend. The second is the process: a machine, a conveyor or a second table has a fixed deck height, and something has to meet it. The first reason is about people and the second is about inches, and a good specification usually has to serve both.

[edt_figure key="scissor-cycle" caption="A single scissor table. The legs swing toward vertical, the platform stays level, and the whole mechanism folds into the lowered height — which is what limits how low the deck can go." alt="A scissor lift table raising and lowering its platform"]

The mechanisms

Nearly everything sold as a lift table is one of five arrangements, and the choice is made for you by the job more often than people expect.

The scissor is the default and by a wide margin the most common: crossed steel legs driven toward vertical by a hydraulic cylinder or an air bag. It spreads the load over a wide base, it folds compactly, and it keeps the platform level throughout. Most of this directory is scissor tables.

Stacked scissors — double and triple — exist because a single scissor's travel is limited by its own folded height. Stacking mechanisms buys height at the cost of footprint, stability at full extension and price. The tallest tables listed here reach just over fifty feet, which is mezzanine work rather than bench work.

The single post puts the deck on one central hydraulic column instead of a folding mechanism. Nothing is underneath the platform, so the deck can rotate freely and lock at any height, which suits welding and machining. The trade is that the column and its base occupy the space a scissor would fold into: the lowest post table in this directory still sits just under twenty inches off the floor.

Tilters angle the platform rather than raise it, so the contents of a deep container can be reached without leaning in. Many are lift-and-tilt, which is what a picking station usually actually needs.

Air bag tables replace the cylinder with an inflating bellows. Few moving parts, no hydraulic fluid, easy to wash down, and travel limited by how tall the bag can get.

How they are powered

The mechanism decides what the table can do; the power source decides whether anybody will use it.

  • Electric-hydraulic is the production default: a motor drives a pump, the operator presses a button. Right for anything cycling more than a few times an hour.
  • Manual means a hydraulic foot pump. Self-contained, cheap, nothing to plug in, and tiring — a full-travel lift with a heavy load can be thirty pumps or more.
  • Air needs no electricity at the table, which is why it appears in spray booths, wash-down areas and anywhere a cord would be a hazard.
  • Battery is for tables that move. Push-button lifting with no trailing cord, at the cost of remembering to charge it.

The four numbers

Four specifications eliminate most of the catalog before anything subjective comes into it.

  1. Capacity. Published models here run from 50 lb to 135,000 lb. The median is 4,000 lb, and 2,000 lb and 4,000 lb between them account for about a third of everything listed.
  2. Lowered height. How low the deck goes decides how the load gets on, and it is the specification buyers reach last and should reach first.
  3. Travel, or raised height. Whichever the manufacturer publishes; the other follows. Measure the destination rather than buying the tallest table available.
  4. Platform size. Size it to the largest load, not to the pallet — cartons overhang pallets routinely.

Across the 4,503 models in this directory that publish a lowered height, the median is 10.5 inches. That is higher than a loaded pallet jack can reach, which is why how the load gets on is a decision in its own right.

What a lift table is not

Three neighboring machines get called lift tables and are not, and ordering the wrong one is an expensive week.

A dock lift bridges the gap between a truck bed and a warehouse floor. It is rated and built for vehicle loading, usually pit-mounted, and it is not a workstation. A stacker or straddle lift carries a load on forks and is a mobile handling machine with a mast; it moves loads rather than presenting them. And a work positioner in the strict sense is a fixed-height fixture, not a lift.

The genuinely blurred edge is the pallet positioner, which is a lift table with a spring or pneumatic mechanism that sinks as each layer is added and rises as each is removed, holding the top of the stack at a constant height with no controls at all. Those are in this directory, filed under pallet lift tables, because they are lift tables — they simply do their controlling by physics.

Where to start

If you know the weight and you know where the load comes from, you can narrow 4,707 models to a handful in about ten minutes. Start with the capacity guide if the weight is the open question, or with loading options if getting the load onto the platform is.

pages.title: How to choose a lift table capacity
pages.excerpt: Why the number on the badge is not the number that matters, how off-center loading changes it, and what capacities are actually available.
pages.content:
Capacity looks like the easy specification. Weigh the load, buy the next size up, done. It is the one that most often turns out to have been chosen wrongly, and almost never because somebody could not do the arithmetic. It goes wrong because a rating describes a particular condition, and the table then spends its life in a different one.

What capacities actually exist

Ratings are not a continuum. Manufacturers build to a handful of standard numbers, and knowing which ones saves specifying a capacity nobody makes.

[edt_figure key="capacity-bands" wide="1" caption="Every model in this directory that publishes a rated capacity, grouped in bands. 2,000 lb and 4,000 lb alone account for 1,531 models — about a third of the catalog. Read from the manufacturers' published specifications, September 2026." alt="Bar chart of 4,674 lift table models by rated capacity, peaking in the 2,000 and 4,000 pound bands"]

The practical consequence is that 2,000 lb and 4,000 lb are where competition, availability and short lead times live. A 3,000 lb requirement is usually better served by a 4,000 lb table than by hunting for an exact match: there are 726 models at 4,000 lb and 227 at 3,000.

Above about 6,000 lb the pattern changes. Tables stop being catalog items and start being engineered per order, which is why heavy duty tables come with approval drawings and a real lead time. Ten percent of the models here are rated 20,000 lb or more, and essentially all of them are built to order.

A rating describes one condition

Published capacity is normally quoted for a load spread evenly over the platform, at the lowered position, static. Three things move it, and all three are common.

Off-center loading. A load sitting toward one end of the platform loads the mechanism unevenly, and the allowable weight drops.

[edt_figure key="offcenter-load" caption="The direction of the effect. How steeply a given table derates off center depends on the design, so the number has to come from the manufacturer — but the number for your load position is the one that matters, not the one on the badge." alt="A load sliding from the center of a lift table platform toward one end, with the allowable capacity bar shrinking as it goes"]

This matters most on single-post tables, where the column carries the load as a cantilever and an eccentric load applies a bending moment it has to resist. It matters least on a wide, squat scissor. If the load will sit anywhere but the middle, ask for the rating in that position.

Rolling loads. A pallet jack or cart driven onto the platform arrives as a moving point load on small wheels, which is a different case from the same weight set down by a forklift. Some tables are rated for it and some are not.

Dynamic and shock loads. A press stroke, a load dropped the last few inches, a robot placing a part — none of these are the static case. If the table is part of a machine cycle rather than a place to put things, say so when specifying.

Ask one question and it will surface all three: "what is the rated capacity with the load in the position and manner I have described?" A supplier who answers with the badge figure has not read the question.

Duty cycle is not capacity, and it is the one people forget

Two tables rated 4,000 lb can be completely different machines. One raises twice a shift; the other cycles every two minutes on an assembly line. The second needs a power unit rated for continuous duty, a mechanism designed for the cycle count, and bearings and bushings chosen accordingly.

Duty cycle is the specification most often left out of an enquiry and the one that decides whether the table is still working in five years. Give the cycles per hour and the hours per day. If the table is being replaced, say what happened to the old one.

How much margin

Buying well over the requirement is not free. A heavier table costs more, weighs more, often has a higher lowered height, and its mechanism may be less sensitive at light loads. Buying under is worse. Some practical rules:

  • Add the container, not just the contents. A steel stillage or a wire cage can be several hundred pounds before anything goes in it.
  • Use the heaviest thing that will ever go on it, including the one-off job somebody will do without asking.
  • Do not use margin to cover an unknown load case. If you are not sure whether the load is central or rolling, resolve that instead — margin against the wrong condition is not margin.
  • Round up to a standard rating rather than specifying an odd one, for the availability reasons above.

What to send a supplier

Everything above reduces to six lines in an email, and a distributor who has these can quote accurately first time:

  1. Heaviest load including its container or pallet
  2. Its footprint, and where it will sit on the platform
  3. How it gets on and off — forklift, pallet jack, cart, conveyor, by hand
  4. Lowered height available, and raised height required
  5. Cycles per hour and hours per day
  6. The environment: indoors, wash-down, freezer, spray booth, outdoors

If any of those is genuinely unknown, say so rather than guessing — a supplier can work with an unknown and cannot work with a wrong number.

pages.title: Getting the load on: low profile, floor level, pit or ramp
pages.excerpt: Most lift tables sit too high for a pallet jack to reach. The four ways round it, what each costs, and the measurement that decides between them.
pages.content:
Here is the single most common expensive mistake in specifying a lift table. The capacity is right, the platform is right, the travel is right, the table arrives — and there is no way to get the load onto it, because the deck sits ten inches off the floor and the only thing available to move pallets is a hand pallet jack.

It is not a rare edge case. It is the default outcome of specifying a lift table on capacity alone.

[edt_figure key="loading-heights" caption="A loaded pallet jack, lowered, rides its pallet a little over two inches off the floor. The median lift table deck sits at 10.5 inches. Nothing rolls on at that height — the deck has to come down to meet it, or the load has to arrive another way." alt="A pallet jack alongside a lift table whose deck lowers from ten inches to floor level"]

The numbers

A folding scissor mechanism has to go somewhere when it folds, and that thickness is the lowered height. Across the 4,503 models in this directory that publish one:

  • 8.5% come down below 6 inches
  • 4.3% reach below 1 inch, which is true floor level
  • 33% sit between 12 and 20 inches
  • The median is 10.5 inches

So roughly nine models in ten cannot be loaded by a pallet jack without something changing. That is a property of the mechanism, not a failing of the manufacturers — and it is why this decision has to be made before the rest of the specification, not after.

Option one: a forklift

If a forklift or a powered stacker is available every time the table is loaded, the whole problem disappears and a standard table at 7 to 12 inches is the cheapest, most available, most heavily competed option in the catalog. Take it.

The question to ask honestly is whether the forklift really is always available. A table that needs a forklift at a station that has one truck shared across a building will be loaded by hand instead, which is the injury the table was bought to prevent.

Option two: a low profile table

Low profile tables are built to fold into a few inches — the lowest here closes to about three-eighths of an inch — so a pallet jack can roll straight on, usually up a short ramp.

Two things to know before choosing one. First, measure the jack, not the pallet: whether it can get on depends on its wheel diameter and frame height, not the pallet's dimensions. Second, a thin mechanism means shallow legs and small pins, and the capacity ceiling comes down with it — low profile tables here top out around 4,400 lb, against 135,000 for scissor tables generally. If the load is a die, this is not the option.

Option three: a floor level table

Floor level tables — also sold as ground entry — lower to the floor with no ramp at all, usually on a U-shaped or E-shaped platform with an open side the jack drives into. The mechanism sits outside or alongside the deck rather than under it.

Three things decide whether one will work. The open side has to face the way the operator approaches, which sounds obvious and is routinely wrong on the order. The throat has to clear the truck, measured across the widest point including its wheels, not the pallet. And the slab has to be flat: a deck designed to close on the floor will rock or bind on concrete that slopes.

Option four: a pit

Set a standard table in a recess so its platform is flush with the floor and you get true floor level at full capacity, with the widest choice of tables and no compromise on the mechanism. What it costs is concrete work, a drawing, and a permanent hole in your floor.

A pit is the right answer more often than it gets chosen, because the concrete quote arrives separately from the table quote and so never gets compared. Price both. If you need floor level and more than a few thousand pounds, a pit-mounted standard table is frequently cheaper overall than a specialist low profile one — and it will outlast the building.

Pits bring their own requirements: drainage, a way to get at the mechanism for service, and guarding around an opening that a platform closes into. Ask about all three at quotation.

Choosing between them

The decision is almost entirely made by two facts you already have.

  1. What moves the load today? Forklift every time — standard table. Hand pallet jack — low profile, floor level or pit. Cart or by hand — low profile is usually enough. Conveyor — neither; match deck heights instead.
  2. How heavy? Under about 4,000 lb opens up low profile. Above it, floor level or a pit.

Then confirm the fit with a tape measure rather than a catalog: the lowered height of the table, against the underside of a loaded pallet on your own jack. Those two numbers decide it, and both take five minutes to get.

If the load arrives on a pallet and gets built or broken down by hand, look at pallet positioners as well — a self-leveling table holds the top of the stack at a constant height with no controls at all, which solves the reaching problem the same trip.
